g.text: N1 [Context]
Scaling LLMs improves performance
Recent research has demonstrated that scaling large language models (LLMs)
by increasing model capacity and expanding training data consistently leads
to significant performance improvements on a wide range of downstream tasks
(Kaplan et…
g.title: N1 [Context] (cites=5) Recent research has demonstrated that scaling large language models (LLMs) by increasing model capacity and expanding training data consistently leads to significant performance improvements on a wide range of downstream tasks (Kaplan et al., 2020; Brown et al., 2020; Henighan et al., 2020; Hoffmann et al., 2022; Dubey et al., 2024).

g.text: N2 [Context]
Scaling = high engineering cost
Scaling introduces substantial operating and engineering costs for both
inference and training.
g.title: N2 [Context] (cites=0) Scaling introduces substantial operating and engineering costs for both inference and training.

g.text: N3 [Context]
Training: synchronous SGD needs bandwidth
In general, training is achieved on a large number of nodes via synchronous
gradient descent techniques, which relies on high-bandwidth communication to
scale.
g.title: N3 [Context] (cites=0) In general, training is achieved on a large number of nodes via synchronous gradient descent techniques, which relies on high-bandwidth communication to scale.

g.text: N4 [Context]
Inference: multi-node needs low latency
Inference of large models may require multiple compute nodes to distribute
the model, which relies on low-latency communication.
g.title: N4 [Context] (cites=0) Inference of large models may require multiple compute nodes to distribute the model, which relies on low-latency communication.

g.text: N5 [Context]
SOTA interconnects critical
In both cases, state-of-the-art interconnect hardware is critical, and
careful engineering is required to scale, and maintain a large compute
cluster.
g.title: N5 [Context] (cites=0) In both cases, state-of-the-art interconnect hardware is critical, and careful engineering is required to scale, and maintain a large compute cluster.

g.text: N6 [Context]
Well-interconnected nodes are privileged access
While mainstream machine learning frameworks have eased the engineering work
on the scaling side, access to a large number of well interconnected nodes
remains a privilege in the machine learning community.
g.title: N6 [Context] (cites=0) While mainstream machine learning frameworks have eased the engineering work on the scaling side, access to a large number of well interconnected nodes remains a privilege in the machine learning community.

g.text: N7 [Method]
Goal: cut communication, keep inference efficient
In this paper, we explore strategies to mitigate the communication
cost of large language models, both at training and inference,
while keeping the inference efficient.
g.title: N7 [Method] (cites=0) In this paper, we explore strategies to mitigate the communication cost of large language models, both at training and inference, while keeping the inference efficient.

g.text: N8 [Method]
Claim: efficient w/o fast interconnects
We show that efficient training and inference can be achieved without
relying on fast interconnects, and without compromising model performance,
both in terms of perplexity or downstream task accuracy.
g.title: N8 [Method] (cites=0) We show that efficient training and inference can be achieved without relying on fast interconnects, and without compromising model performance, both in terms of perplexity or downstream task accuracy.

g.text: N9 [Prior_Work]
PW line 1: reduce gradient sync
In recent studies aimed at mitigating reliance on high-bandwidth
interconnects, researchers have developed algorithms that reduce
the need for frequent or comprehensive gradient synchronizations.
g.title: N9 [Prior_Work] (cites=0) In recent studies aimed at mitigating reliance on high-bandwidth interconnects, researchers have developed algorithms that reduce the need for frequent or comprehensive gradient synchronizations.

g.text: N10 [Prior_Work]
Async training + gradient compression
Such techniques include asynchronous training (Douillard et al.,
2023; Aji & Heafield, 2017; Zhang et al., 2015; Liu et al., 2024)
and gradient compression (Lin et al., 2017; Dettmers, 2016) which
effectively decrease communication…
g.title: N10 [Prior_Work] (cites=6) Such techniques include asynchronous training (Douillard et al., 2023; Aji & Heafield, 2017; Zhang et al., 2015; Liu et al., 2024) and gradient compression (Lin et al., 2017; Dettmers, 2016) which effectively decrease communication overhead.

g.text: N11 [Prior_Work]
Methods cut comms, keep throughput
By performing updates less frequently or by communicating less
data, these methods sustain high training throughput while
diminishing dependence on high-speed interconnects.
g.title: N11 [Prior_Work] (cites=0) By performing updates less frequently or by communicating less data, these methods sustain high training throughput while diminishing dependence on high-speed interconnects.

g.text: N12 [Limitation]
Still need sync; underperform every-step
However, these algorithms still require some level of gradient
synchronization, and resulting models often under perform (in
terms of perplexity) compared to training approaches synchronizing
at every step (Diskin et al., 2021).
g.title: N12 [Limitation] (cites=1) However, these algorithms still require some level of gradient synchronization, and resulting models often under perform (in terms of perplexity) compared to training approaches synchronizing at every step (Diskin et al., 2021).

g.text: N13 [Prior_Work]
PW line 2: sparse activation MoE (Switch)
Regarding efficient inference, a number of sparse parameter
activation techniques have recently become popular (Shazeer et
al., 2017; Fedus et al., 2022; Artetxe et al., 2022; Lewis et al.,
2021; Du et al., 2022), in particular the Switch…
g.title: N13 [Prior_Work] (cites=5) Regarding efficient inference, a number of sparse parameter activation techniques have recently become popular (Shazeer et al., 2017; Fedus et al., 2022; Artetxe et al., 2022; Lewis et al., 2021; Du et al., 2022), in particular the Switch Transformer mixture of experts (MoE).

g.text: N14 [Prior_Work]
MoE reduces active inference params
These approaches are effective at reducing significantly the
number of active model parameters at inference time.
g.title: N14 [Prior_Work] (cites=0) These approaches are effective at reducing significantly the number of active model parameters at inference time.

g.text: N15 [Limitation]
MoE: per-token routing needs fast interconnect + RAM
Yet, they require routing decisions to be made for each token,
demanding rapid interconnections and requiring all parameters to
be accessible in RAM.
g.title: N15 [Limitation] (cites=0) Yet, they require routing decisions to be made for each token, demanding rapid interconnections and requiring all parameters to be accessible in RAM.

g.text: N16 [Prior_Work]
PW line 3: async training mixtures of models
To achieve both low-bandwidth training and efficient inference,
several prior works have explored asynchronously training mixtures
of models (Gross et al., 2017; Li et al., 2022; Gururangan et al.,
g.title: N16 [Prior_Work] (cites=3) To achieve both low-bandwidth training and efficient inference, several prior works have explored asynchronously training mixtures of models (Gross et al., 2017; Li et al., 2022; Gururangan et al., 2023).

g.text: N17 [Prior_Work]
K-Means clustering on input space
In these methods, the input space is clustered using unsupervised
techniques like K-Means, with each model in the mixture trained on
an assigned cluster.
g.title: N17 [Prior_Work] (cites=0) In these methods, the input space is clustered using unsupervised techniques like K-Means, with each model in the mixture trained on an assigned cluster.

g.text: N18 [Prior_Work]
Cut comms, improve perplexity, same inference
These approaches reduce communication overhead and have
demonstrated improvements in model perplexity, while maintaining
similar inference costs to baseline models (Gross et al., 2017;
Gururangan et al., 2023).
g.title: N18 [Prior_Work] (cites=2) These approaches reduce communication overhead and have demonstrated improvements in model perplexity, while maintaining similar inference costs to baseline models (Gross et al., 2017; Gururangan et al., 2023).

g.text: N19 [Limitation]
Need full-corpus clustering or metadata; debate on
short-prefix tasks
However, in the context of language processing, their practical
applicability on standard downstream tasks with relatively short
input prefixes remains a subject of debate, as they rely on full
corpus clustering or access to metadata (Li…
g.title: N19 [Limitation] (cites=2) However, in the context of language processing, their practical applicability on standard downstream tasks with relatively short input prefixes remains a subject of debate, as they rely on full corpus clustering or access to metadata (Li et al., 2022; Gururangan et al., 2023).

g.text: N20 [Method]
Introduce SmallTalkLM (async + sparse)
In this paper, we introduce SMALLTALK LM, an asynchronous mixture
of language models, which combines the advantage of asynchronous
LM training methods (significantly reducing interconnect
requirements), and sparse activation methods (it…
g.title: N20 [Method] (cites=0) In this paper, we introduce SMALLTALK LM, an asynchronous mixture of language models, which combines the advantage of asynchronous LM training methods (significantly reducing interconnect requirements), and sparse activation methods (it naturally uses only a subset of the overall architecture parameters during inference).

g.text: N21 [Result]
Beats dense baseline at same FLOPs
SMALLTALK LM achieves better perplexity, and better accuracy on a majority
of downstream tasks, compared to a regular dense language model trained with
the same amount of FLOPs.
g.title: N21 [Result] (cites=0) SMALLTALK LM achieves better perplexity, and better accuracy on a majority of downstream tasks, compared to a regular dense language model trained with the same amount of FLOPs.

g.text: N22 [Contribution]
C1: independent-LM mixture algorithm
We introduce an algorithm that trains a mixture of independent
language models, significantly reducing bandwidth requirements
during training compared to regular distributed training methods.
g.title: N22 [Contribution] (cites=0) We introduce an algorithm that trains a mixture of independent language models, significantly reducing bandwidth requirements during training compared to regular distributed training methods.

g.text: N22b [Contribution]
C1b: lightweight router (<1.5% expert size)
Our approach leverages a lightweight router (which accounts for
less than 1.5% of the size of each expert) to efficiently route
sequences.
g.title: N22b [Contribution] (cites=0) Our approach leverages a lightweight router (which accounts for less than 1.5% of the size of each expert) to efficiently route sequences.

g.text: N22c [Contribution]
C1c: routes via short prefix
This router determines the most suitable expert for a given
sequence based on a short prefix (see § 2).
g.title: N22c [Contribution] (cites=0) This router determines the most suitable expert for a given sequence based on a short prefix (see § 2).

g.text: N23 [Contribution]
C2: lower perplexity vs dense at same FLOPs
We empirically demonstrate that our method achieves significantly
lower perplexity than a dense baseline for near-identical training
and inference FLOPs and identical training data volume (see Fig.
g.title: N23 [Contribution] (cites=0) We empirically demonstrate that our method achieves significantly lower perplexity than a dense baseline for near-identical training and inference FLOPs and identical training data volume (see Fig. 2).

g.text: N23b [Contribution]
C2b: improvement scales with #experts
Furthermore, we show that for a constant mixture model size, the
improvement in perplexity increases with the number of experts.
g.title: N23b [Contribution] (cites=0) Furthermore, we show that for a constant mixture model size, the improvement in perplexity increases with the number of experts.

g.text: N24 [Contribution]
C3: ≥dense on 75% of downstream tasks
We evaluate our method on a set of downstream tasks, showing that
it achieves better or similar accuracy compared to a dense
baseline on 75% of the tasks (see § 3.3 and App. B).
g.title: N24 [Contribution] (cites=0) We evaluate our method on a set of downstream tasks, showing that it achieves better or similar accuracy compared to a dense baseline on 75% of the tasks (see § 3.3 and App. B).
